book_intro:
Blue Letter Bible bakanlığı ve BLB Enstitüsü, Kutsal Yazıların tahrif edilemezliğine olan kesin inancı da içeren tarihsel, muhafazakar Hristiyan inancına bağlıdır. BLB tarafından sağlanan metin ve ses içeriği çeşitli Evanjelik gelenekleri temsil ettiğinden, kaynak materyallerde aktarılan tüm fikir ve ilkelerin bu bakanlık tarafından toplamda onaylanması gerekmez.

Blue Letter Kutsal Kitap çalışma araçları Kutsal Kitap'ı okumayı, araştırmayı ve çalışmayı kolay ve ödüllendirici hale getirir.

notes.text: a temple for the name of the Lord. See Deut. 12:5. God’s “name” in association with a place signifies that he chooses to be present there among his people. Yet God is not just present in the temple. He is present everywhere (2 Chron. 2:6). royal palace. Linked here with the temple, perhaps to indicate the close connection between the two “houses” of the Davidic covenant (see 1 Chron. 17:14).
Solomon used the forced labor of Canaanites (see vv. 17–18; see notes on 8:7–10; 1 Chron. 22:2–5) for building the temple.

Solomon’s letter to Hiram, king of Tyre (who had earlier assisted David; 1 Chron. 14:1), is considerably expanded from 1 Kings 5:3–6. This letter describes the purpose of the temple for worship according to the Law of Moses, it expresses the supremacy of Israel’s God (2 Chron. 2:5–6), and it requests a skilled craftsman (v. 7) and different kinds of timber (v. 8).
heaven, even highest heaven, cannot contain him. See note on 1 Kings 8:27–30.
In his reply to Solomon, Hiram, though a Gentile, acknowledges Yahweh as Creator.
